The house I grew up in had a room we called the “unfinished room.” It was above the garage, a space my father had intended to turn into a study. He had started with great enthusiasm. He’d run the electrical wiring, hammered up drywall, and even installed a large, south-facing window that looked out over our scraggly backyard and the alley beyond. But then, life happened. The money ran out, or the motivation did, or perhaps the two are always intertwined. The room remained a skeleton. The drywall was unpainted, a pale, dusty grey. The floor was bare plywood, save for a constellation of stray nails and curled-up tubes of caulk. Exposed wires dangled from the ceiling like metallic tendrils, waiting for a fixture that never came.

As a child, this room was my cathedral, my laboratory, my sanctuary. It was a place of pure potential. It wasn't a study, which would have been a room for a specific, adult purpose. It was a void, and a void can be anything. It was a spaceship navigating the cosmos, the command center for a global spy network, a medieval keep, an alien landscape. The lack of finish was not a defect; it was the defining feature. The room’s power was in its incompleteness. It was a physical manifestation of “what if,” and I spent countless hours in that dusty, sun-drenched space, building worlds out of nothing.

I’ve come to believe that this is the fundamental state of our existence. We are all, in our own ways, unfinished rooms. The myth of the finished product—the completed human, the perfect career, the settled life—is just that: a myth. We are taught to chase it, to measure ourselves against some imaginary blueprint of completion, but the truth is that we are, and always will be, a work in progress. The beauty, the terror, and the profound opportunity of a life lie not in its final coat of paint, but in its exposed wiring, its bare floors, and the vast, echoing potential of its empty space.

This state of incompleteness is perhaps most visible in the world of art. We venerate the finished masterpiece: Michelangelo’s *David*, flawless and serene in his marble perfection; da Vinci’s *Mona Lisa*, a portrait so complete it seems to hold a living soul within its varnish. We see them in museums, behind glass, as immutable objects of perfection, and we forget the chaos of their creation. But for every finished masterpiece, there are countless others that exist in a state of tantalizing suspension.

Think of the “non-finito” technique of Michelangelo. His series of unfinished slaves, struggling to break free from the blocks of marble, are arguably more powerful than his finished works. In their rough-hewn state, you can see the sculptor’s mind at work. You can feel the immense effort of the struggle between the artist’s vision and the unyielding stone. The figures are not yet fully formed; they are emerging. Their incompleteness is their narrative. They are a perfect metaphor for the human spirit, forever striving to emerge from the raw material of our own potential. A finished slave would be a static sculpture. An unfinished one is a story of creation itself.

Or consider literature. We mourn the books that were never written. We are obsessed with the fragments of Sappho’s poetry, the tantalizing gaps in her lines forcing us to imagine what words, what emotions, once filled them. Our engagement with the text becomes an act of creation. We are not just passive readers; we are collaborators, completing the work in our own minds. This is perhaps the most intimate relationship we can have with art. The unfinished work demands something of us. It requires our participation. It respects our intelligence and our imagination. It says, “I have taken you this far. The rest is up to you.”

We see this too in the tantalizing final works of artists. Franz Schubert’s “Unfinished” Symphony is one of his most beloved compositions, precisely because of its two completed movements. It doesn’t feel like a failure. It feels like a perfect, self-contained world that has been left ajar, a door opened to a vista we can only glimpse. The mystery of why he stopped—was it a crisis of confidence, a loss of interest, a simple diversion?—becomes part of the music itself. The silence that follows the second movement is not an empty void but a profound, pregnant pause filled with everything that might have come next. The potential, the “what if,” becomes more potent than any possible musical resolution.

The 20th-century composer Charles Ives took this a step further with his *Universe Symphony*. He worked on it for decades, a sprawling, cosmic concept that aimed to capture the entirety of existence in sound. He left it as a collection of sketches, a chaotic jumble of musical ideas, notes, and celestial diagrams. He knew it could never be finished, not in any conventional sense. The idea was too vast for any human lifespan. To listen to the various attempts to perform it is to experience a beautiful, magnificent failure. It is the sound of a human mind reaching for the infinite and falling short, but the reach itself is the art. The *Universe Symphony* is not a piece of music; it is an act of philosophical inquiry, a career-long question mark left for all of us to ponder.

I find a strange comfort in these unfinished artifacts. They liberate us from the tyranny of the perfect. In a world that constantly pushes us toward completion—the perfect ending, the flawless final product—they remind us that there is profound beauty and honesty in the process. The sketchbook, with its smudged false starts and half-realized ideas, is often more interesting than the pristine final painting. The first, messy draft of a novel is often more alive with raw energy than the polished, published version.

The celebration of incompleteness is a running theme through much of Eastern philosophy as well. The Japanese concept of *wabi-sabi* is a worldview centered on the acceptance of transience and imperfection. It finds beauty in the flawed, the imperfect, and the incomplete. A cracked tea bowl, repaired with veins of gold (*kintsugi*), is more beautiful than a flawless one because its history, its fragility, and its repair are made visible. Wabi-sabi is not about slapping a coat of paint over the cracks; it’s about celebrating the cracks themselves as part of the object’s story. It is the antithesis of the Western ideal of perfect, pristine, and permanent. It teaches us to see our own lives not as projects to be flawlessly completed, but as gardens to be tended, where weeds and flowers grow together, where seasons change, and where there is always something new emerging from the soil.

This idea of a life as a garden, not a monument, is a powerful antidote to the pressure of the “finished self.” We are not static objects. We are processes. Our identities are not set in stone. We are a collection of habits, beliefs, memories, and desires that are constantly in flux. The person I was at 20 is a stranger to me now, but his unfinished dreams and clumsy mistakes are part of the foundation of who I am today. To claim to be “finished” is to declare that you have stopped growing, stopped learning, stopped changing. It is a kind of death.

The unfinished room of my childhood was a gift because it taught me this lesson before I had the language for it. I learned that the best things are not always the perfect things. I learned that a space can be filled with imagination long before it’s filled with furniture. I learned that the question is often more beautiful than the answer.

Now, as an adult, I see these “unfinished rooms” everywhere. I see them in the half-built sentences of my own writing, which I sometimes leave hanging, not out of laziness, but out of a desire to let an idea linger, unresolved. I see them in the abandoned ambitions of friends, the career paths they didn’t take, the relationships they didn’t pursue. We tend to look at these things with a sense of regret or failure. But what if we looked at them differently? What if we saw the abandoned path not as a dead end, but as a story that simply wasn’t meant to have a conventional ending? What if the road not taken still has its own, invisible, terrain?

We live in a culture of doers, of finishers. We celebrate the entrepreneur who takes an idea and brings it to market. We praise the student who graduates. We buy the book with the definitive conclusion. This is not necessarily a bad thing; it is the energy that builds bridges and cures diseases. But it is only one half of the story. The other half is the story of the tinkerer, the dreamer, the philosopher, the artist. The half that values the process over the product, the journey over the destination.

My father, for better or worse, was a man who lived in the unfinished room. He was a man of grand ideas and fleeting enthusiasms. His garage was a graveyard of unfinished projects: a half-built sailboat, a car engine perpetually on the verge of being repaired, the plans for that study upstairs. As a child, I saw this as a flaw. Now, I see it as a facet of a creative, restless spirit. He was not a finisher, but he was a starter. He was a man who lit fires and then stood back, mesmerized by the flames, before wandering off to light another. His life was a collection of magnificent, unfinished rooms. He never wrote a book or built a business, but he filled his head with thousands of ideas, and he shared them with a passion that was, in its own way, a kind of completion of thought.

The German poet Rainer Maria Rilke understood this deeply. In his *Letters to a Young Poet*, he advises the young man to “have patience with everything unresolved in your heart and to try to love the questions themselves as if they were locked rooms or books written in a very foreign language. Don’t search for the answers, which could not be given to you now, because you would not be able to live them. And the point is, to live everything. Live the questions now. Perhaps then, someday far in the future, you will gradually, without even noticing it, live your way into the answer.”

This is the great wisdom. To live the questions. To embrace the state of being an unfinished room. It is a call for radical patience. It is a rejection of the frantic need to have it all figured out. It is a faith that the process of living itself is more important than any conclusion we might reach. The “answers” are not final destinations. They are just new, slightly more complex questions.

This is not, of course, an argument for laziness or for giving up. It is not an excuse to abandon responsibility. It is an argument for a shift in perspective. It is about seeing the beauty and integrity in the process, even when the end result is uncertain or elusive. It is about honoring the struggle, the doubt, the mess, and the raw, unpolished beauty of something that is still becoming.

Think of the human brain, the most complex object in the known universe. It is not a finished project. It is a mass of neural pathways that are constantly being pruned and reinforced. It is in a perpetual state of becoming. Neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life, is perhaps the ultimate biological proof of our unfinished nature. We are wired for growth, for change, for adaptation. We are not a finished product; we are a dynamic, evolving system.

And what of the universe itself? Our understanding of cosmology points to an ever-expanding cosmos, a universe that is not a static, finished cathedral but a process, a story that is still being written. We are not living in a finished creation. We are moments within an ongoing act of creation. We are stardust that has become conscious of itself, and that consciousness is not a final state. It is an emerging property, an event of cosmic significance that is still unfolding.

So perhaps the ultimate act of humility and of hope is to accept our own unfinished state. To stop pretending that we have all the answers. To stop feeling like a failure because our life doesn’t look like a perfectly rendered painting. To embrace the half-built sailboat, the unresolved question, the unpainted wall. To find the beauty in the bare floor and the dusty sunlight of our own unfinished rooms.

My father never finished the room above the garage. But I can still feel the rough texture of the drywall under my fingertips. I can still smell the sawdust. I can still see the light streaming through that large window, illuminating the dust motes dancing in the air, each one a tiny, perfect, unfinished world. It was the most complete room in the house. It was a sanctuary of potential, and its lesson was simple: the story is never over. The wall is never truly finished. The room is never truly complete. The most profound act, the most beautiful creation, is to simply be living within its unfinished walls, breathing in the dusty air, and asking, with patience and with love, “What comes next?”
